lines: You wake up in the ruins of a settlement. Nobody has lived here for a long time.
Your throat is dry. Everything you need starts with clean water.
Look around. Anything you find might help.
A pool of water. It is cloudy, and there is a sheen on the surface.
You can not trust it. Drinking it could make you sick.
The old treatment unit nearby might be fixable. You will need materials.
Still untreated. Repair the treatment unit first.
Clear, cold, and safe. The treatment unit works.
Fixing one system made another one usable.
The treatment unit hums to life. The filter holds.
Reused metal, a recovered pipe, and a plastic filter housing. Nothing new was made.
A cracked recorder. You press play.
"Day 412. We keep saying someone else will deal with the waste."
"It was never one disaster. It was a thousand small choices to look away."
"If you can hear this, follow the old pipeline north. There is a source of pure water. They call it the Last Drop."
The path north is closed off. You still have things to find here first.
The old battery factory. Rusted shelves, cracked crates, a smell of chemicals.
Careful here. Some of this is dangerous.
The generator coughs, then catches. Lights flicker on across the factory.
A terminal wakes up. It is linked to something far away.
The terminal is dead. It needs power.
ARCHIVE LINK ESTABLISHED. THE LAST SANCTUARY.
You expected to find who destroyed the world. A villain. A machine. A single mistake.
There was none. The collapse took decades. Industry chose cheap over clean. Waste systems were neglected. Policies were postponed.
"Humanity did not lose the world because it had no solutions. It lost the world because it repeatedly chose not to use them."
And the Last Drop is not a magic spring. It is a restoration facility, built to heal water, soil and ecosystems.
It needs maintenance, knowledge, and people working together. It is a place to start again.
You keep the archive for your own community.
A small group is safe, for now. The rest of the world is left waiting.
You release the archive and invite every community to the Last Drop.
It will be hard to coordinate, and the knowledge may be misused. But restoration can finally begin.
You sorted carefully, and it showed. The systems you repaired still work.
You made some mistakes along the way, and learned from each. The repairs held.
Too many things were thrown away carelessly. The world remembers, and the repairs will be harder.
Towers rise out of the plastic like broken teeth.
Whatever people threw away, they never stopped throwing.
Sorting here is slow and tedious. It is also the only way to build anything.
Another recorder, wedged in a pile of old phones. You press play.
"Day 301. We had sorting plants. Good ones. Then someone realised it was cheaper to ship the waste away than to fix them."
"Away has an address. It is always someone else's backyard."
"The river is next. Follow the green stain, and do not drink it."
The river is the colour of old tea. The air tastes of metal.
A treatment plant waits on the far bank, its basins dry.
Clear water is not the same as safe water. Learn the difference.
A recorder, dripping, on the riverbank.
"Day 188. The plant needed new filters. The budget meeting went on for two years."
"Everyone knew. Everyone agreed it was serious. Nobody voted for the cost."
"Plants do not fail. People defer them."
Nothing grows here. Not because it is dry, but because the soil forgot how.
Soil is alive. Without life it is just dust.
Maybe the dump has something to give it back.
A recorder, wrapped in a seed packet.
"Day 120. We stopped feeding the soil. We fed the crops instead. It worked, until it did not."
"Waste was always just food for something else. We forgot that."
"The factories will tell you the rest. Be careful what you open."
The chimneys are cold. The signs still warn you.
Some of this is treasure. Some of it is poison. The labels will tell you which.
Do not guess.
A recorder, hung on a fence beside a warning sign.
"Day 60. We measured success by how much we made. Never by what it cost to make it."
"The cheapest product always had a hidden bill. Someone else paid it. You are standing in it."
"The Sanctuary is in the hills. The door still opens for anyone who brings power."
Moss grows on the glass. Someone kept the lights on, once.
Every region you crossed left something here. Piece it together.
Fragment: Overconsumption.
Buy, use, discard. The loop was never closed.
Fragment: Neglected recycling.
Plants closed. Collection stopped. Landfills filled.
Fragment: Delayed action.
Policy was postponed again, for good reasons each time.
Fragment: Hidden costs.
Cheap goods. Poisoned rivers. Different people paying.
Fragment: Collective inaction.
Everyone waited for someone else to move first.
There was no single catastrophe.
Humanity did not lose the world because it had no solutions.
It lost the world because it repeatedly chose not to use them.
You look for a spring. There isn't one.
The Last Drop is a restoration facility: research, equipment, water systems, seed banks.
It will not rebuild the world by itself. It needs people, power and patience.
The last recorder, on the console.
"Day 1. If you are listening, you found it. You powered it. That means you already know how."
"It does not fix anything on its own. It is a tool. It needs hands."
"The world was not destroyed in a single day. It will not be rebuilt in one either."
"What you do with this place is up to you."
You seal the archive and keep it safe.
Your community will be protected. The wider world will have to wait.
You open the channels and send everything out.
Some will answer. Some may misuse it. Nothing is certain, but the door is open.
ARCHIVE LINK UNSTABLE. Most records are corrupted.
One fragment survives: a municipal waste report. Sorting plants closed. Collection stopped.
A line of coordinates points to the Great Dump, beyond the north gate.
The roof panel locks in. Rain will stay out and warmth will stay in.
Cardboard for insulation, cloth for the seals, metal for the frame. Three kinds of waste, one shelter.
A small solar cell on the roof hums. Somewhere in the dump, a terminal wakes.
A municipal terminal wakes on the shelter's solar cell.
Waste routes, closure dates, budget notes. Every plant that closed has a signature, and every signature has a reason.
Nobody here was a villain. Everyone expected someone else to act.
One last file names a river and a treatment plant that never got its filters. Where the dump drains, the river begins.
Upstream. The water looks clear.
The strip says otherwise: a faint stain of dissolved metals.
Clear does not mean safe.
Below the dump's drain. Cloudy and green.
The strip turns dark: metals and runoff from the heaps.
Rain carried it here. Where waste goes, water follows.
Downstream. A rainbow sheen floats on top.
The strip shows chemicals that no amount of boiling will remove.
Boiling kills germs. It does not clean poison.
Cloth, charcoal, sand and pipe lock into the old filter bed.
Four recovered materials, one working stage. But a filter alone is not a plant.
The console beside it needs the stages set in order.
The pumps shudder, then run. Water moves through each stage in turn.
The final strip stays pale. For the first time in years, this water is safe.
Downstream, the river is still grey. But there is a place to start.
Slow grey water at the bank. Cloudy, with a sheen.
You cannot drink it. The treatment plant on the north bank might clean it.
Still untreated. Install the filter and start the treatment cycle.
Clear, cold, and tested. The strip stays pale.
One river, one plant, and a lot of work still ahead.
